_comment: QUESTION deck — words only. Filed from docs/active/investigations/2026-09-21-conversation-lease-handoff-audit.md.
Plain-language rule: this deck says 'handoff' and 'hold on a conversation' rather than the code's own word for the lease.
Pages: 1 = how claiming should work, 2 = what the app says, 3 = direction calls.
title: Live conversation handoff — the questions before any building

steps.page: How claiming a conversation should work
steps.intro: When you open a conversation that another of your devices is using, the two devices agree on who keeps writing. These three decide how that agreement should behave.

steps._comment: Q-1 — the atomic-admission decision (audit H1/H4): claim before opening vs open then correct.
steps.path: Settings → Backup & Sync; opening a conversation that lives on your other devices
steps.headline: Should the app hold a conversation before it opens it, rather than after?
steps.today: When you open a conversation that lives on your other devices, the app checks nobody else is using it, opens it, and only then claims it as yours to write in.
steps.problem: In the moment between opening and claiming, another of your devices can claim it first. When that happens, both devices keep typing into the same conversation with no warning on either one. The audit found this is reachable on a perfectly healthy connection, not just when sync is down.
steps.proposal: Two shapes for the fix. Claim-then-open holds the conversation first and shows it second. Open-then-correct opens as fast as today and corrects your screen a moment later if another device won.

options.label: Claim, then open
options.summary: Opening waits a moment while the app claims the conversation; only then does it appear.
pros: The moment you are typing, it is yours — nobody can slip in.
cons: Opening a conversation now leans on sync being reachable; a slow connection can delay it.
A new way to fail exists: if the claim cannot complete, you see a message instead of the conversation.
options.measured: the claim adds one round trip, well under the 25 s handoff budget

options.label: Open, then correct
options.summary: Opening stays instant; if the claim is lost, your screen corrects itself a second later.
pros: Opening never waits for the network.
cons: You can type for a few seconds into a conversation you are about to be moved out of.
Needs every lost-claim path to actually fire — the same paths the audit found being ignored.

steps._comment: Q-2 — what the losing device sees when admission fails.
steps.path: Opening a conversation that another device just claimed
steps.headline: If another device wins the conversation while you are opening it, what should your screen do?
steps.today: Your window opens the conversation as if nothing happened. Both copies keep updating separately and silently.
steps.problem: You can type into a conversation that is already live somewhere else, and your words and the other device's words end up on two different copies with no sign of it.
steps.proposal: Opening would stop with a short message — 'this conversation moved to your other device'. Pick what your screen does after the message.

options.label: Open the other copy
options.summary: You are told it moved, and the app opens the newest copy — the one your other device has been using.
pros: You still get the conversation, with everything the other device wrote.
cons: A screen you did not ask for appears where the conversation you picked was.

options.label: Message only
options.summary: You are told it moved and you stay where you were, on the list of conversations.
pros: Nothing opens that you did not ask for.
cons: You find and open the conversation again yourself.

options.label: Let me take it anyway
options.summary: The message offers the same 'take over anyway' choice the handoff dialog already has, for when the other device is not really in use.
pros: Covers the case where the other device is idle and nobody is losing anything.
cons: One more decision at the exact moment the fast path failed, and easy to misuse.

steps._comment: Q-3 — the expired-hold split-brain (audit H5): what a waking device does.
steps.path: A device that was asleep, or a laptop that was closed, coming back to a conversation
steps.headline: When a device wakes up and its hold on a conversation has expired, whose copy should win?
steps.today: A device holds a conversation while it works on it. If it sleeps long enough, its hold quietly expires and another device can take the conversation over — and when it wakes, both sides believe they own it.
steps.problem: The waking device keeps typing into a conversation the other device now owns. Neither side knows. The words end up on two different copies of the conversation.
steps.proposal: The waking device would check whether someone took over while it slept, and something would give. Pick what gives.

options.label: Other device wins
options.summary: The waking device checks, sees it lost, and steps aside at once.
pros: The device that stayed awake never sees its conversation pulled out from under it.
No dialog when you open a laptop.
cons: If you were about to use the waking device, it points you at the other copy instead.

options.label: Waking device wins
options.summary: The waking device takes the conversation back the moment it can.
pros: You pick up exactly where you left off, wherever you were.
cons: The other device's newer work is set aside into a separate copy.
Who wins depends on which device woke last, not on what you meant to do.

options.label: Waking device asks
options.summary: A dialog on wake: 'this conversation moved to your other device — step aside or keep it?'
pros: You decide per conversation, not by rule.
cons: A popup every time a slept device wakes into a moved conversation.

steps.intro: These five decide the warnings and the words — the part you asked to see made transparent.

steps._comment: Q-4 — audit F1/F4: the hub-down silence.
steps.path: Opening a conversation when the sync service cannot be reached
steps.headline: If the app can't reach the sync service, should opening a conversation warn you?
steps.today: Everything about 'is another device using this conversation' is checked through the sync service. If the service cannot be reached, the check is skipped with no message, and opening looks completely normal.
steps.problem: On a flaky connection or when sync is down, the protection is silently off: you can open a conversation your other machine is live in, and nothing anywhere tells you the safety net is missing.
steps.proposal: A small, non-blocking note — 'couldn't check your other devices' — would appear when the check can't run. Yes adds it; No keeps the silence.
steps.risk: The note will show up on every launch with poor internet until sync recovers, so it has to stay calm and dismissable.

steps._comment: Q-5 — audit F3: the (i) popup explanation.
steps.path: Settings → Backup & Sync → the (i) next to the panel's title
steps.headline: How much should the Backup & Sync (i) popup explain about live conversations?
steps.today: The (i) popup explains sync, backups and conflicts, but says nothing about what happens when two devices have the same conversation open.
steps.problem: The handoff dialog is the only place the rules appear, and it appears mid-task — you learn how handoffs work at the exact moment one is going wrong.
steps.proposal: Three sizes for the explanation. Pick how deep it should go.

options.label: Short paragraph
options.summary: Two or three sentences: the same conversation on two devices means one device is asked to hand it over, and the other keeps a separate copy.
pros: Reads in seconds, and the popup keeps its size.
cons: Leaves out the failure cases — sync down, forced takeovers, the phone.

options.label: Full section
options.summary: A titled section: handoffs, separate copies, the moved pill, and when protection is unavailable (sync down, phones).
pros: Everything in one place; nothing has to be discovered mid-failure.
The audit already drafted this copy.
cons: The popup gets noticeably longer, for something most sessions never hit.

options.label: Link out
options.summary: One line in the popup plus a link to a fuller explainer page.
cons: Another page to write and keep current.

steps._comment: Q-6 — audit F7: the hidden consequence in the first dialog.
steps.path: The dialog you get when opening a conversation another device is using
steps.headline: Should the handoff's first dialog name the separate-copy consequence up front?
steps.today: The first dialog says what is about to happen, and the fact that the other device keeps its own separate copy is only on a hover tip.
steps.problem: Most people never hover. The one consequence you cannot undo — the other device's copy forking — is the one hidden.
steps.proposal: One line inside the dialog: 'Your other device keeps working in its own separate copy.' Yes adds it; No leaves it hover-only.

steps._comment: Q-7 — audit M1: the 'didn't answer' overstatement.
steps.path: The handoff dialog, after a handoff times out
steps.headline: The dialog says your other device "didn't answer" when really it couldn't confirm — what should it say?
steps.today: When a handoff times out, the dialog says your other device was asked to hand over the conversation but didn't answer.
steps.problem: The system cannot always know the other device was reached at all, so on a slow connection the dialog can blame a device that never got the message.
steps.proposal: Pick the wording that should replace 'didn't answer', or write your own under Other.

options.label: Couldn't confirm
options.summary: You would see: 'We couldn't confirm the handoff. Your other device may still be using this conversation.'
pros: Never blames a device that may never have been reached.

options.label: Say the current fact
options.summary: You would see: 'The conversation is still held by your other device.' Nothing about messages at all.
pros: States what is true right now, which is what decides your next step.
cons: Does not say that an attempt was made.

steps._comment: Q-8 — the client half of H3: the 'final changes still arriving' state.
steps.path: Top of a conversation, just after another device handed it over
steps.headline: When a handoff takes longer than expected, should the conversation say 'final changes still arriving'?
steps.today: During a handoff the new device waits up to 25 seconds for the old device's last updates, then opens the conversation with whatever arrived.
steps.problem: If the old device's final push is slow or fails, you start from an older version of the conversation and the missing tail shows up later as a separate copy — with nothing telling you that is why.
steps.proposal: A small pill at the top of the conversation — 'final changes still arriving' — would show while the last updates are in flight and quietly clear when they land. Yes adds it; No keeps opening with whatever arrived, no pill.

steps.intro: Three decisions that shape what gets built, and in what order.

steps._comment: Q-9 — audit H6: Android's place in the feature.
steps.path: The Android app, using conversations on the device itself
steps.headline: Should the phone stay outside live handoff for now, with copy saying so plainly?
steps.today: The handoff dialog, the moved pill and the warnings work between desktops. The phone app does not take part: it can open a conversation your desktop is live in with no warning at all — and its own 'resume' starts fresh rather than continuing the conversation (a separate known bug).
steps.problem: The feature is described as cross-device, but on the phone it does not exist, and nothing tells you that — so the gap looks like the app failing rather than a decision.

options.label: Copy says so
options.summary: The (i) popup and the dialog state plainly that live handoffs work between desktops; the phone joins when its rebuild lands.
pros: Honest today, and costs only words.
No new scope on a large project already in flight.
cons: The phone still has no protection — just an explanation of why.

options.label: Fix in rebuild
options.summary: The Android rebuild picks up handoffs as part of its scope, so the phone eventually gets the same protection.
cons: Nothing changes on the phone until the rebuild lands, which is a long tail.
Adds scope to a rebuild that is already large.

steps._comment: Q-10 — audit M2: the worker identity gap.
steps.path: The sync service that carries handoffs and sync between your devices
steps.headline: Should the sync service refuse a device id that doesn't match the signed-in connection?
steps.today: The sync service trusts whatever device a handoff message says it is from, and only the sign-in itself is checked.
steps.problem: Anything running inside your account could pretend to be one of your other devices — taking over, renewing or letting go of its conversations. It is your account's door, not an outside one, but the room behind it is unlocked.
steps.proposal: The service would check the device named in the message against the signed-in device and refuse mismatches, with a test proving a forged one is refused. Yes fixes it; No leaves it open.

steps._comment: Q-11 — the build order this session proposed and you approved in chat.
steps.headline: Does this order work: quick fixes first, the rewrite next, the new states last?
steps.today: The audit left four groups of work: two quick fixes (the sync service identity check, the transparency copy), a rewrite of how conversations are claimed (desktop plus sync service), and new visible states for handoffs.
steps.problem: Building all of it as one thing would take weeks before you saw anything, and the quick fixes would sit behind the rewrite.
steps.proposal: The order: 1) the identity check and the transparency copy as two small fixes, 2) the claim rewrite, 3) the new states. You review each group on its own branch. Yes goes in that order; No means tell me your order in the note.
